nameStory: Common dogwood gets its "bloody" nickname from its striking red winter twigs that look like they've been dipped in crimson paint. The name "dogwood" itself comes from "dag wood" - referring to the hard, dense wood that was once carved into "dags" (sharp pointed tools) and skewers.
description: Common dogwood is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-12 feet tall and wide. This European native is occasionally found in New England as an ornamental plant that has sometimes escaped cultivation. It's most famous for its brilliant red or purplish-red winter stems that provide stunning color in the dormant season, paired with clusters of small white flowers in summer and dark berries in fall.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems turn brilliant red to deep purplish-red in winter, feeling smooth to the touch - this dramatic color is most intense on newer growth and makes the plant unmistakable in the dormant season

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves grow in opposite pairs with prominent curved veins that arc from the midrib toward the leaf tip - they feel smooth and papery, turning reddish or purplish before dropping in fall

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers cluster together in flat-topped groups about 2-3 inches across in early summer, each flower having four petals and a slightly sweet scent

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dark purple to black berries ripen in late summer, feeling firm and slightly waxy - they're bitter to taste and arranged in clusters where the flowers once bloomed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a rounded, somewhat spreading shrub with multiple stems arising from the base - branches arch gracefully outward and feel flexible when young

habitat: Common dogwood is rarely found wild in New England, but may occasionally escape from cultivation in suburban and urban areas where it's planted as an ornamental. When it does naturalize, it typically grows in disturbed soils along roadsides, woodland edges, or abandoned garden sites with partial sun to shade.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late spring, and you can see the winter's brilliant red stem color starting to fade as the growing season begins.
seasonality.summer: Flat-topped clusters of small white flowers bloom in early summer, followed by green berries that gradually darken. The red winter color is barely visible on actively growing stems.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn reddish or purple before dropping, and berries ripen to dark purple-black. The spectacular red color begins returning to the bare stems.
seasonality.winter: This is showtime - the bare red to purplish-red stems create a stunning display against snow and gray skies, making identification easy even from a distance.

funFact: Common dogwood's winter stem color is so prized by gardeners that they often cut the shrub nearly to the ground each spring - this "coppicing" forces new growth that produces the most intensely colored red stems the following winter.
confusionNotes: The brilliant red winter stems make this nearly impossible to confuse with anything else, but red osier dogwood (a native species) also has red winter twigs. Red osier dogwood typically grows in wetter areas and has slightly different bark texture - common dogwood's stems are smoother and often more purplish-red.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "common" dogwood, this species is actually quite uncommon in New England since it's not native here. Most dogwoods you'll encounter in our region are native species like gray dogwood or flowering dogwood, making this European import a special find when discovered.
compareHints: Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark. Red osier dogwood is the closest match for winter color, but grows in wetlands rather than upland sites where common dogwood typically escapes cultivation.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
